analytic.title: Designing Multimedia Applications on Real-Time Systems with SMP Architecture *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Large real-time multimedia systems such as flight simulators have adopted multiprocessor architecture to handle the large amount of events and computations. Existing realtime scheduling algorithms designed for single-processor systems such as Rate Monotonic (RM) and Earliest Deadline First Algorithm (EDF) have very poor performance on multiprocessor systems. On the other hand, most online scheduling algorithms for multiprocessor systems have poor schedulability conditions for real-time applications. In this paper, we study different ways to design real-time applications on SMP machines.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: With the rapid advent of computer technology, computer processor size is getting smaller, computing speed is faster, computer systems more reliable, yet the cost is getting lower. It is now possible to apply sophisticated but inexpensive computer-aided solutions to complex multimedia applications such as flight simulators and advanced skill trainers. Many simulator systems have adopted multiprocessor architecture to handle the large number of system events and the large volume of computation data that are typical in this ytpe of systems. With an appropriate system design, the SMP (Symmetric Multi-Processors) architecture allows a system to be more scalable and more reliable. SMP-based systems are more scalable since the number of processors can be increased with the growing needs of the application (assuming the hardware support is builtin.) SMP-based systems can be more reliable since the unavailability of one processor will not affect the execution of the other processors if the system can re-adjust the workload assigned to each processor.

However, existing optimal real-time scheduling algorithms designed for single-processor systems such as Rate Monotonic (RM) and Earliest Deadline First Algorithm (EDF) have a very poor performance on multiprocessor systems. Moreover, most on-line schedulers for SMP systems cannot be used to meet real-time scheduling constraints. In this paper, we study the scheduling frameworks for SMPbased multimedia systems. We compare many well-known scheduling frameworks and see how they may be used.

We also propose to use the concept of scheduling group for real-time scheduling on SMP machines. A scheduling group contains a set of jobs that share the available budget for the group. We present the group scheduling support on RED-Linux [15] and show its effectiveness running practical multimedia applications.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the objectives of designing high performance multimedia systems. Section 3 presents the requirements of a real-time flight simulator. Section 4 introduces the scheduling framework supported in RED-Linux. In Section 5, we present different system frameworks for structuring multimedia systems on SMP and compare their pros and cons. Section 6 shows how to use the group scheduling mechanism for SMP architecture. The paper is concluded in Section 7.

div.head: Objective of High Performance Multimedia Application Framework
div.p: Many multimedia systems have been implemented and deployed. However, a successful multimedia system should adopt a theoretically sound design framework so that it will be easy for the system to grow both in size and in capabilities. In general, a multimedia design framework should have the following properties:

• Analyzability: One of the most important issues for any simulator system is to make sure that the simulated environment can interact with human operator in real time. That means the system must react to any operator input or external clocked event in an acceptable time bound; otherwise the system movement will be sluggish and unrealistic. To ensure this, the system performance must be analyzable given all possible workload in order to provide the guaranteed performance.

• Scalability: Most multimedia systems, when they were first implemented, were designed for simpler functionalities or to be used by a smaller number of users. As systems get more mature, more functionalities or more users will be added. A system design should allow it to grow easily without having to be redesigned completely.

• Portability: With the continuing advancement of computer hardware and architecture technology, systems will need to be ported from one platform to another as an old generation becomes obsolete. A good design framework should allow an easy migration process between platforms.

• Efficiency: No system design framework is a good one if it cannot use the system resource in the most efficient way. The minimization of cost is often the most critical goal for any multimedia system especially if the system is to be produced in large quantity.

• Reliability: Multimedia systems may be used not only in simulators but also in actual devices. For example, most advanced vehicles or aircrafts have automatic steering control functions. A design framework must have some way to ensure or even enhance the system reliability if needed. For real-time systems, some special features to handle system overloads are often necessary.
In this paper, we will evaluate different SMP design frameworks and use the above criteria for comparison.

div.head: A Real-Time Flight Simulator
div.p: The target system of our study is a real-time flight simulator. The training of qualified personnel for missioncritical systems (such as avionics, submarines, armored vehicles, or nuclear power plants) has always relied on sophisticated simulators to reduce both cost and risk. A good simulator must provide a realistic multimedia environment for the person under training. In addition, we can use a simulator to create extreme conditions that may not happen that often in real life so that a trainee have more chances to practice the very demanding, extremely safety critical operations.

For military and security applications, simulators even allow trainees to be in a place that is impossible to enter before the mission starts. For example, a pilot can be trained to fly in an enemy air space before the actual mission. One good example is the training of pilots before the Gulf War. Since pilots had been trained in realistic simulators before the actual campaign, they were all very familiar with the local terrain features in the real mission and achieved great successes.
In general, a flight simulator can divided into the following subsystems:
div.formula: • Host Computer Subsystem • Visual Subsystem • I/O Subsystem • Sound/Communication Subsystem • Instruction Subsystem • Cockpit Subsystem • Motion Subsystem • HLA (High-level Architecture) Subsystem
div.p: All these subsystems will be used to execute different software components, such as visual/audio generator, terrain/landscape database, weapon control, flight control, aerodynamics, cockpit movement, flight electronic, etc. Different software may run on different subsystems. But all software modules (about 20 of them) related to aircraft control are run on the Host Computer Subsystem. Some of the most critical software and their execution frequencies includes: Flight Control (60 Hz), Flight Dynamics (60Hz), Flight Aero (60Hz), Flight 6-degree of Freedom (60Hz), Flight Subsystem (30Hz), Flight Engine (30Hz), Flight Navigation (30Hz), Radar (30Hz), Flight Electronics (30Hz), Weapon Control (30Hz), Target (30Hz), etc. Executions of these software modules are usually defined in frames according to their frequencies. The data flow is shown in Fig. 1. The main input signals are collected from the pilot control pole, accelerator, etc. These analog signals are read by the I/O Subsystem and converted into digital data stored in the local memory. The data will be sent to the Host Subsystem via a high speed data communication interface. To software modules running on the Host, these data are the main inputs that trigger all subsequent executions. After the Host processing, A/V Subsystem will read the data and produce the video to be displayed and also the sound to be produced. The process is repeated in all frames.

From the above description, we can see that there is a strong data dependency between software modules. If any one module cannot complete its operation before the welldefined time frame, the next module in sequence will not have the correct data to process. Even a small deviation in each step may accumulate into an unacceptable system instability or inaccuracy after certain time. Since aircraft data contain more than one hundred thousand double variables, utilizing a good design framework to ensure the correct realtime execution of these software modules is absolutely critical to a flight simulator system.

The goal of this project is to implement a military-grade flight simulator on SMP machines running RED-Linux realtime operating system. Given the above system description, it is desirable to implement a system which is easy to analyze and to scale in the future. In the following sections, we will present an overview of RED-Linux, and discuss design considerations on SMP machines.

div.head: The RED-Linux General Scheduling Framework
div.p: In this section, we provide an overview on the RED-Linux general scheduling framework (GSF) [15]. The goal of the framework is to integrate many well-known scheduling paradigms, including priority driven [8], time driven [5], and share driven [13,6], so that any application can use RED-Linux for real-time support.

div.head: Scheduling Paradigms in RED-Linux
div.p: Most of today's operating systems are designed to have time-sharing capabilities. In Linux, processes are scheduled using the time-sharing approach but assigned with different, dynamic priorities. Multimedia applications, however, require better scheduling support on how system resources are used. In this section, we review how jobs may be scheduled using different scheduling paradigms.

div.head: Time-Driven Scheduling
div.p: For many traditional real-time systems, decisions on when to execute which jobs are made at specific time instances. In this scheduling paradigm, the time instances when each task starts, preempts, resumes and finishes are pre-calculated and enforced by the scheduler. These instances are chosen a priori before the system begins execution. It is therefore easy to predict and to control task behaviors. This paradigm of scheduling is referred as time-driven (or clock-driven). Typically, in a system using the time-driven (TD) scheduling, the parameters of hard real-time jobs are fixed and known. A schedule table of the jobs is computed off-line and is stored for use at run time. The scheduler prioritizes the jobs according to this table at each scheduling decision time. In this way, scheduling overhead during run-time can be minimized.

For systems with steady and well-known input data streams, time-driven schedulers have been used to provide a predictable processing power for each data stream [7]. Applications such as small embedded systems, automated process control, and sensors can be implemented efficiently using this scheduling paradigm. Another feature of TD schedules is the jitter-free property since all executions will be started at precise times and produce results at predictable time instances. For systems with close human interactions, such as robots, intelligent devices and automated environments, predictable and jitter-free executions are desirable or even necessary for human users.

div.head: Priority-Driven Scheduling
div.p: The most common approach to implementing real-time systems is to adopt a periodic process model and use the priority-driven (PD) scheduling paradigm. Priority-driven scheduling is implemented by assigning priorities to tasks. At any scheduling decision time, the task with the highest priority is selected and executed. PD scheduling includes two types of algorithms, fixed priority and dynamic priority scheduling. The most well-known fixed priority algorithm is the Rate-Monotonic (RM) algorithm and the most wellknown dynamic priority scheduling algorithm is the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm [8]. Aperiodic and nonreal-time activities are typically scheduled either as background processes or served by an aperiodic server process by the real-time scheduler.

However, the PD paradigm allows a misbehaving high priority task to overrun and reduce the available CPU bandwidth to tasks at all lower priority levels. When the system becomes overloaded, the scheduler needs some extra mechanisms to control misbehaving tasks. Thus in a PD scheduler, it is critical to have a good admission-control mechanism. In addition, the priority attribute is defined by the timing constraints such as the period length (in RM) or the deadline (in EDF), not the importance of the task. It is difficult to schedule tasks with a long period (or a late deadline) but need a fast response time.

Compared to the TD approach, the PD scheduling approach has several advantages. First, PD schedulers are easy to implement. Many well-known PD algorithms use very simple priority assignments, and for these algorithms, the run-time overhead for maintaining a priority queue of ready jobs can be made very small. A TD scheduler requires a priori information on the release times and execution times of the jobs in order to decide when to schedule them. In contrast, a PD scheduler does not require most of this information, making it much better suited for applications with varying time and resource requirements. One of the most important advantages for PD is that there are the closed-form schedulability checks, so that the admission control is much easier.

div.head: Share-Driven Scheduling
div.p: Recent advances in computing and communication technologies have led to a proliferation of demanding applications such as streaming audio and video players, multiplayer games, and online virtual worlds. A key characteristic of these applications is that they impose (soft) realtime constraints, and require predictable performance from the underlying operating system. For such applications, a share-driven (SD) resource allocation paradigm may be more appropriate. The SD scheduling paradigm is based on the GPS (General Processor Sharing [10]) algorithm. Using the SD approach for OS scheduling, every real-time task is requested with a certain CPU share (or weight). All tasks in the system share the computing resources according to the ratio based on their requested shares.

Several systems have experimented with the share-driven support for real-time networks. In these systems, each application receives a share which, on average, corresponds to a user-specified weight or percentage. Some well-known SD scheduling mechanisms include the Total Bandwidth Server [11], the Constant Bandwidth Server [1], and the Constant Utilization Server [3]. An implementation of the SD scheduler has been reported using the FreeBSD kernel [13,6].

div.head: RED-Linux General Scheduling Framework (GSF)
div.p: Different scheduling paradigms use different attributes to make scheduling decisions. In order for all above paradigms to be supported in the RED-Linux GSF, four scheduling attributes are defined for each job in GSF: priority, start time, finish time, budget. Among the four, the start time and the finish time together define the eligible interval for a job execution. The budget specifies the total execution time assigned to a job. These attributes thus can be used as constraints. However, these timing attributes can also be used as the selection factors when a scheduler needs to select a job to be executed next.

In RED-Linux, we use a two-component scheduler structure. GSF separates the low level scheduler, or the Dispatcher, from the QoS parameter translator, or the Allocator. We also design a simple interface to exchange information between these two components. It is the Allocator's responsibility to set up the scheduling attributes associated with each real-time job according to the current scheduling policy. The Dispatcher inspects each job's scheduling attribute values, chooses one job from the ready queue and dispatches it to execution. In addition to assigning attribute values, the Allocator also determines the evaluation function of scheduling attributes, since each job has multiple scheduling attributes. Using GSF, the Allocator defines the policy and the Dispatcher provides the mechanism. In this way, we are able to separate the scheduling policy from the scheduling mechanism. GSF provides a flexible means so that real-time system developers may choose different scheduling policies tailored to their specific applications. More details on the GSF implementation and the performance measurement can be found in [15].

div.head: RED-Linux Scheduling Group
div.p: Hierarchical scheduler is a new scheduling feature that has received a lot of interest recently [3,15,17]. The idea is useful when building multimedia systems with multiple independent sets of applications, or when jobs are related by sharing some system budget. Hierarchical job structure is especially useful when jobs are restricted to consume some limited set of resources so as not to interfere with other jobs that have received system QoS guarantees.

Jobs in a group (Fig. 2) are either a simple job or another group job, which contains its own group of jobs. Every job has a scheduling budget. But if it belongs to a group, the job's budget is also constrained by its group's budget. A job group number is defined in the RED-Linux general scheduling framework [16]. The group number is used to identify the type of jobs (normal or group) in the Dispatcher queue. A group job has a group of child jobs. When scheduled, a group job will select one of its child jobs in the group for execution. The job selection (scheduling) policy in the group can be defined by the group itself. Since any child job could be again a group, the selection process is repeated recursively. Using this mechanism, hierarchical schedulers of multiple levels can be supported easily.

div.head: Real-Time System Design on SMP
div.p: Although RED-Linux can be used to support many different scheduling paradigms, for people who are designing real-time applications on SMP machines, special care must be taken to make sure the system will not have unexpected behavior. In this section, we present different ways to structure real-time applications on SMP architecture, and the different scheduling methods that may be used.

div.head: Fixed Priority using Rate Monotonic
div.p: One of the most popular scheduling paradigms used is the fixed priority assignment using the rate monotonic (RM) algorithm [8] which assigns higher priorities to jobs with shorter periods. For single-processor systems, it has been shown that n periodic jobs can meet their deadlines as long as the total utilization of all jobs is less than n(2 1/n -1), where the utilization u i of a job is defined to be its execution time divided by its period.

Unfortunately, it has been shown that the scheduling condition for multiprocessor RM (MP-RM) is only u i ≤ 1 no matter how many processors are available. A simple example can be used to show this result: Suppose there are m processors. If a system has m periodic tasks each with a period of 1 ms and execution time of 2 ms, and 1 task with a period of 1 + ms and execution time of 1 ms. The last task will miss its deadline at the first period even though the system has a total utilization close to 1 only.

Using a variation of RM, we can achieve a schedulability condition of m 2 /(3m-2) for m-processor systems. The variation (called RM-US [2]) is to assign a special priority level (the highest in the system) to any task with a utilization ≥ m 3m-2 . The rest of the system is scheduled using the regular RM priority assignment for all periodic tasks. When m is large, the RM-US scheduling condition approaches m/3, much better than the original MP-RM schedulability condition.

Yet another method to schedule periodic real-time tasks using RM is to first divide all tasks into m different subsets, and assign each subset to a specific processor. Since RED-Linux supports CPU-binding, we can bind a subset of tasks to a processor. In this way, the schedulability checking can be done on a per-processor basis. Ideally, all processors can have a schedulability condition of n(2 1/n -1) if the processor has n tasks to run. On the other hand, the division of tasks into multiple processor is a bin-packing problem [4]. When the number of tasks is big, it is difficult to find the best way to divide these tasks. In the worst case, the schedulability condition is around 0.28m [4]. On the other hand, since most real-time systems may not have a large number of tasks nor processors, it is possible to find a reasonable partition which may acheive the optimal SMP schedulability condition of 0.7m. Moreover, when all task periods are harmonic numbers, the single-processor schedulability condition can be as high as 1, or up to m for m-processor systems.

For jobs with data dependency, RM does not provide any mechanism to handle that. To ensure data dependency, we can assign different priorities to different jobs. For example, if two tasks A and B have the same period but A must produce data for B, we can use two priority levels for A and B so that A has a higher priority than B. In this way, A is always run before B in each period thus meeting the dependency requirement. But compared with other tasks with longer periods, A and B must have a higher priority; and vice versa for other shorter period tasks. This works if both A and B run on the same processor. If they are not on the same processor, the precedence relationship cannot be guaranteed.

Finally, systems may need some way to handle the overload situation. On RED-Linux, we can either use the budget attribute to place an upper bound on the execution time for a job or use the group mechanism to bound the budget shared among a set of jobs. If jobs are partitioned and assigned to different processors, the overload on one processor will not affect the execution of other processors. A system designer should use special care when partitioning the task set.

div.head: Deadline Driven Scheduling
div.p: Multiprocessor EDF (MP-EDF) has a similar problem as MP-RM with a schedulability condition of 1 regardless of how many processors are available. In fact, the same worst case example given in the last section for MP-RM can be used to show the worst case behavior for MP-EDF as well. Therefore, one can use the partition approach to divide the tasks into m subsets on an m-processor system. As long as the total utilization in each subset is less than 1 the system is schedulable.

If no task partition is used, two extensions of the EDF algorithm have been designed. The first is called EDF-US [12], which assigns the highest priority to any task with a utilization ≥ m/(2m -1) while the rest of the system is scheduled by regular EDF. It has been shown the schedulability condition of EDF-US is m 2 2m-1 for m processors, or around m/2 for large m.

The second EDF extension is called EDZL which requires the system to keep track of all active jobs' laxity values (laxity is defined to be the difference between a job's remaining execution time and the remaining time to its deadline). When a job's laxity drops to 0, the job is immediately promoted to the highest priority and executed without interruption. Using EDZL, it has been shown that the schedulability condition is 3m/4 for m processors.

For data dependency, since EDF scheduler does not use priority, we cannot use different priorities to enforce the execution order. However, we may assign a slightly different deadline to enforce the execution order. In other words, in RED-Linux GSF, every job that is to be executed before another should be given an earlier finish time even if two jobs have the same period. For example, we may assign one to have a deadline of P (i.e. the period) while its predecessor has a deadline of P -. The shortened deadline enforces an earlier execution but will not change the system load. The schedulability checking should still use the original period length.

The overload management for EDF is similar to RM in that we can either use the budget constraint for each job or a group of jobs. Different from RM, EDF is less stable than RM since any overloaded job may affect the whole system (or at least for those jobs sharing the same CPU). In comparison, using RM, only those jobs with lower priorities will be affected by an overloaded job. Therefore, overload management is a must in EDF-based systems.

div.head: Time Driven SMP
div.p: Using the time driven framework, all jobs are defined with their start times and finish times. As long as the actual execution time is less than the specified budget, all jobs can be guaranteed to meet their deadlines. On the other hand, if a job cannot finish its execution using the given budget, the system may handle it in three ways: either the job is aborted, delayed to the next period, or another job is delayed to allow the job to finish. Using any of the options, the system will suffer some performance degradation. If the job is aborted, unless the job is able to produce some imprecise result [9], those jobs that have data dependency on this job will not have any new data for their processing. On the other hand, if the job continues its execution, some other jobs may receive less time than their original budgets. This may have the domino effect and cause many jobs to miss their deadlines. The option of delaying the job execution until the next period will isolate the overload effect to the job only. However, it still has the problem of not producing a valid output for those jobs waiting to use the result.

As a result, most time-driven schedules assign a large budget for jobs whose outputs are critical to the system function. The problem with an over-allocated execution budget is the possible system inefficiency. If a job has a much shorter execution time than what it is assigned, no other job will be able to use the leftover budget since all jobs' executions are defined in other time intervals. Therefore, the system is under-utilized in order to avoid missing deadlines.

Using time-driven scheduling, data dependency between jobs can be handled by setting the schedule accordingly. Since job schedule is strictly followed, this is not a problem. On the other hand, any change on data dependency may require a schedule to be re-constructed.
In general, as long as the execution time estimate is not precise, time-driven scheduling is not a good design framework for either single processor or multiprocessor multimedia systems.

div.head: CBS-Based Share-Driven Scheduling
div.p: For multimedia tasks, each task should be allocated some well-defined CPU bandwidth to guarantee the smooth execution of multimedia applications. The CBS algorithm [1] can be used to provide such a guarantee. In such a system, CBS servers are defined with some fixed share of the CPU bandwidth. Each CBS server can be described by (Q i , P i ), where Q i is the maximum budget, and P i is the period of the server. The ratio U i = Qi Pi is the fraction of CPU bandwidth reserved for the server. Dynamically, each server S i maintains a pair of parameters: (c i , d i ), where c i is the budget available for S i , and d i is current scheduling deadline of S i . Each multimedia task is associated with a CBS server, and thus all its ready jobs are assigned to the server. However, more than one tasks may be assigned to a server. Each server has a job list which includes all jobs to be served on this server. If the job list is not empty, then the server is said to be active; otherwise, it is idle.

The system consists of many CBS servers. A low level kernel scheduler based on the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling policy is used to select the active server with the budget that has the earliest deadline. For SMP systems, CBS servers may be pre-assigned to specific processors to avoid the MP-EDF scheduling problem.

The most important property of CBS is the bandwidth isolation property which ensures that each CBS server S i will consume the system utilization for no more than U i if the system is fully-or over-loaded. The misbehavior of some task will not jeopardize other tasks' bandwidth allocation. Therefore, overloads can be handled automatically.

CBS-based scheduling does not have any good way to handle data dependency, except by delaying a job from en-tering its CBS server's ready queue until the predecessor job is finished. This can be accomplished in RED-Linux by using the Allocator to detect the predecessor's finish event.

div.head: Comparisons of Frameworks
div.p: Let us now compare the design frameworks presented above. Our comparison will be based the design objectives presented in Section 2, namely, analyzability, scalability, portability, efficiency and reliability.

We have already presented the schedulability conditions of all different frameworks. Among them, the time-driven framework is the most difficult to analyze, and also the most sensitive to the accuracy of execution time estimation. Both MP-RM and MP-EDF can be analyzed easily with MP-EDF has a slightly better condition than MP-RM. CBS is usually based on EDF and can be analyzed easily. In terms of efficiency, CBS has the best condition but is designed mainly for soft real-time systems. MP-EDF has the best schedulability condition, thus can give the most efficient system.

For scalability consideration, again time-driven is the least flexible since any change on the number of tasks or processors may require a complete re-construction of the system schedule. Both MP-EDF and MP-RM can easily facilitate new tasks. If the partition approach is used, as long as a new task does not require the system to be re-grouped into new partitions, MP-EDF and MP-RM are easily scalable. Data dependency can also be added (by creating a new priority level or deadline) if a new task needs it. MP-CBS can assign new CBS servers to serve new tasks as long as the data dependency requirement is not very strict.

For portability, all except time-driven are reasonably portable. MP-RM and MP-EDF require the execution budget to be revised to test for schedulability on the new system. In this sense, CBS is the most portable since all tasks will be given proportional budgets depending on the total workload in a system.

div.head: Group Scheduling on SMP
div.p: For large real-time multimedia systems such as real-time simulators, different parts of a real-time system may be used to perform different functions for applications. A subset of the tasks may need to share some computing or data resources with each other closely. Therefore, systems usually divide tasks into groups that are functionally related. Each group is then managed as a unit. This will reduce the system complexity and increase the system efficiency. None of the above scheduling paradigms has taken this approach.

With the hierarchical scheduling group mechanism in RED-Linux, multimedia applications can be managed in a hierarchical manner. Each multimedia task group (or sub-group) can be bound to a specific processor and preallocated well-defined CPU budget to guarantee its smooth and successful operations. By using hierarchical grouping, we can control the resource consumption of a subsystem without understanding how the subsystem allocates and schedules resources among its various independent activities. We simply control the total budget used by the group. This provides extra, unmatched convenience when porting systems from one architecture to another. For example, suppose we want to port a legacy SMP system, that currently provides satisfactory real-time functions, to a new architecture. Using the group mechanism, we can simply put all tasks that used to run on a processor as a group. When porting to the new system, the group will not need to be changed. The group can be guaranteed to perform successfully as long as the new system provides enough CPU bandwidth to the group as a whole. In this way, we can easily reduce the porting effort from managing all jobs to managing only the groups.

For multiprocessor systems, group scheduling provides a natural way of partitioning system into subsets of system. Since each subset of tasks need to share certain resources, it is natural to allocate these tasks to the same processor. We may use heuristic solutions to bind groups to processors. Each processor then uses optimal local scheduling algorithms designed for single processor to guarantee groups' real-time performance. Group scheduling is independent of the specific scheduling policy used by each group. Therefore, it can be integrated with different frameworks to create a rich structure. In fact, each group may decide what scheduling algorithm to use inside the group. For SMP systems, each processor can have its own scheduler. Therefore, we can have one processor running RM to achieve the stability for high-priority jobs, another processor using EDF to have a better utilization, while a third to use CBS servers to handle soft real-time jobs. For systems with dynamic or non-real-time workloads, they can be scheduled using a global scheduler. Whenever any CPU has idle time but does not have pre-defined local real-time job to run, the global scheduler can use the time to execute soft or non-real-time jobs.

Data dependency cannot be handled by group scheduling. It should be handled by each group scheduler (such as RM or EDF). Overloads are insulated on the group boundary. If we map groups to processors, those sharing a processor may suffer the overloads in the same processor unless CBS is used.

We believe the group scheduling provides the best solution for building multimedia systems on SMP. Such systems are analyzable, since each group scheduler can be analyzed independently. They are scalable, since new tasks can be added a group or new sub-groups can be formed easily under an existing group. They are portable since each group may be ported and verified independently. With a group scheduler, each processor can be utilized efficiently. For those jobs without processor binding, we can also use a global scheduler to make use of any leftover CPU time. Finally, reliability can be achieved by budget control and replicated groups.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have studied the issues on designing multimedia applications on SMP machines. Several design frameworks, based on the schedulers used, have been presented and compared. We have also presented the groupbased framework which provides an analyzable and scalable solution for real-time applications on SMP machines. Using RED-Linux, a user may choose what scheduling paradigm to use and may design application-dependent schedulers. Many difficult issues on SMP scheduling can be resolved by such flexible schedulers. The flight simulator project is being implemented. More experience on this system design and implementation will be reported in the future.
